claim: The amphipod crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis is a blossoming model system for studies of developmental mechanisms and regeneration.
source: The amphipod crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis is a blossoming model system for studies of developmental mechanisms and more recently regeneration.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about Parhyale's use in research.

claim: Parhyale is a member of the Malacostraca clade, which includes crustacean food crop species.
source: Parhyale is a member of the Malacostraca clade, which includes crustacean food crop species.
evidence: This is a direct statement about Parhyale's taxonomic classification and the composition of the Malacostraca clade.

claim: Parhyale and other species within Multicrustacea contain the enzyme sets necessary to perform lignocellulose digestion.
source: We also find that Parhyale and other species within Multicrustacea contain the enzyme sets necessary to perform lignocellulose digestion ('wood eating'), suggesting this ability may predate the diversification of this lineage.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of glycosyl hydrolase genes in the genome presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Parhyale genome is the first malacostracan genome sequenced.
source: The first malacostracan genome will underpin ongoing comparative work in food crop species and research investigating lignocellulose as an energy source.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key contribution of the work.

claim: The Parhyale genome is estimated to be 3.6 Gb in size.
source: At an estimated size of 3.6 Gb, this genome represents one of the largest animal genomes tackled to date.
evidence: This is based on k-mer analysis and assembly statistics presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Parhyale genome is the second largest reported arthropod genome after the locust genome.
source: The Parhyale genome contains 23 pairs (2n=46) of chromosomes (Figure 2) and with an estimated size of 3.6 Gb, it is currently the second largest reported arthropod genome after the locust genome (Parchem et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citation to the locust genome publication.

claim: Parhyale has 23 pairs of chromosomes (2n=46).
source: The Parhyale genome contains 23 pairs (2n=46) of chromosomes (Figure 2)
evidence: This is supported by karyotyping experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Forty-six chromosomes were observed in more than half of all mitotic spread preparations.
source: Forty-six chromosomes were observed in more than half of all preparations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A which displays the frequency of chromosome counts.

claim: The Parhyale genome exhibits very high levels of heterozygosity, similar to the highly heterozygous oyster genome.
source: We concluded that the single sequenced adult Parhyale exhibits very high levels of heterozygosity, similar to the highly heterozygous oyster genome (see below).
evidence: This is based on k-mer frequency analysis showing a bimodal distribution.

claim: The frequency of variant branches in the Parhyale genome is 10x higher than that observed in the human genome.
source: We found that the frequency of the variant branches was 10x higher than that observed in the human genome and very similar to levels in the highly polymorphic genome of the oyster Crassostrea gigas (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on k-mer branching analysis comparing Parhyale to other species.

claim: The frequency of repeat branches in the Parhyale genome is approximately 4x higher than those observed in both the human and oyster genomes.
source: We also observed a frequency of repeat branches approximately 4x higher than those observed in both the human and oyster genomes (Figure 3C), suggesting that the big size of the Parhyale genome can be in large part attributed to the expansion of repetitive sequences.
evidence: This is based on k-mer branching analysis and supports the inference about genome size.

claim: 57% of the Parhyale genome assembly consists of repetitive elements.
source: We found 1473 different repeat element sequences representing 57% of the assembly (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on RepeatModeler and RepeatMasker analysis of the genome assembly.

claim: The final Parhyale genome assembly comprises 133,035 scaffolds, 259,343 unplaced contigs, and 584,392 shorter potentially allelic contigs, with a total length of 4.02 Gb.
source: The Parhyale assembly comprises of 133,035 scaffolds (90% of assembly), 259,343 unplaced contigs (4% of assembly), and 584,392 shorter, potentially allelic contigs (6% of assembly), with a total length of 4.02 Gb (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of assembly statistics.

claim: The N50 length of the Parhyale scaffolds is 81,190 bp.
source: The N50 length of the scaffolds is 81,190 bp.
evidence: This is a direct report of an assembly metric.

claim: The final Parhyale genome annotation resulted in 28,155 gene models.
source: This resulted in 28,155 final gene models (Figure 4B; Source code 3)
evidence: This is based on Augustus gene prediction trained with transcriptome data and other evidence.

claim: The Parhyale canonical proteome consists of 28,666 proteins.
source: For downstream analyses of Parhyale protein coding content, a final proteome consisting of 28,666 proteins was generated by combining candidate coding sequences identified with TransDecoder (Haas et al., 2013) from mixed stage transcriptomes.
evidence: This is based on combining transcriptome-derived coding sequences with gene predictions.

claim: 244 out of 248 CEGMA orthology groups were identified from the assembled Parhyale genome alone.
source: We identified 244/248 CEGMA orthology groups from the assembled genome alone and 247/248 with a combination of genome and mapped transcriptome data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on CEGMA analysis to assess genome completeness.

claim: 96% of over 280,000 identified transcripts mapped to the assembled Parhyale genome.
source: Additionally, 96% of over 280,000 identified transcripts, most of which are fragments that do not contain a large ORF, also mapped to the assembled genome.
evidence: This is based on mapping transcriptome data to the genome assembly.

claim: Parhyale has a mean coding gene size of 20 kb (median of 7.2 kb).
source: Parhyale has a mean coding gene size (introns and ORFs) of 20 kb (median of 7.2 kb), which is longer than D. pulex (mean: 2 kb, median: 1.2 kb), while shorter than genes in Homo sapiens (mean: 52.9 kb, median: 18.5 kb).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene structure in the genome annotation.

claim: The mean intron size in Parhyale is 5.4 kb.
source: The mean intron size in Parhyale is 5.4 kb, similar to intron size in H. sapiens (5.9 kb) but dramatically longer than introns in D. pulex (0.3 kb), D. melanogaster (0.3 kb) and C. elegans (1 kb) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of intron sizes in annotated genes.

claim: Genes in the lower coverage region (<105x coverage) have a higher level of heterozygosity (2.68%) than genes in the higher coverage region (1.09%).
source: Genes that fell within the higher read coverage group had a lower mean heterozygosity (1.09% of bases displaying polymorphism), which is expected as more reads were successfully mapped. Genes that fell within the lower read coverage group had a higher heterozygosity (2.68%), as reads mapped independently to each haplotype (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is based on analysis of read coverage and heterozygosity in transcribed regions.

claim: The rate of additional variations in transcribed regions from the laboratory population is not substantially different between genes from the higher (0.88%) versus lower coverage group genes (0.73%).
source: In addition to polymorphisms that agreed with heterozygosity in the genome sequence we observed that the rate of additional variations is not substantially different between genes from the higher (0.88%) versus lower coverage group genes (0.73%; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcriptome data from multiple laboratory populations.

claim: SNPs were detected at a rate of 1.3 to 2.5% among the Parhyale Hox BAC clones.
source: We detected SNPs at a rate of 1.3 to 2.5% among the BACs (Table 3)
evidence: This is based on mapping genomic reads to BAC sequences.

claim: Parhyale encodes 6 of the 13 Wnt subfamily genes: wnt1, wnt4, wnt5, wnt10, wnt11 and wnt16.
source: The Parhyale genome encodes 6 of the 13 Wnt subfamily genes; wnt1, wnt4, wnt5, wnt10, wnt11 and wnt16 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on identification of Wnt genes in the genome annotation.

claim: Parhyale wnt1 and wnt10 are linked in a single scaffold.
source: We observed that wnt1 and wnt10 are linked in a single scaffold (phaw_30.0003199); given the loss of wnt6 and wnt9, this may be the remnant of the ancient wnt9-1-6-10 cluster conserved in some protostomes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene positions in the genome assembly.

claim: Parhyale has 2 Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF) genes and only a single FGF receptor (FGFR).
source: We could identify 2 Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF) genes and only a single FGF receptor (FGFR) in the Parhyale genome, suggesting one FGFR has been lost in the malacostracan lineage (Figure 8——figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on identification of FGF pathway genes in the genome.

claim: Parhyale has a single decapentaplegic homologue among the BMP genes.
source: Of the BMP genes, Parhyale has a single decapentaplegic homologue (Figure 8—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on identification and classification of BMP genes.

claim: A genome wide survey identified a total of 1143 transcription factors with DNA binding domains in Parhyale.
source: A genome wide survey to annotate all potential transcription factors (TFs) discovered a total of 1143 proteins with DNA binding domains that belonged to all the major families previously identified.
evidence: This is based on domain-based identification of transcription factors.

claim: Parhyale has 699 ZF-C2H2-containing genes.
source: Parhyale has 699 ZF-C2H2-containing genes (Chung et al., 2002–12], which is comparable to the number found in H. sapiens (Najafabadi et al., 2015), but significantly expanded compared to other arthropod species like D. melanogaster encoding 326 members (Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on identification of zinc-finger transcription factors in the genome.

claim: The Parhyale genome contains 126 homeobox-containing genes.
source: The Parhyale genome contains 126 homeobox-containing genes (Figure 9; Figure 8—source data 3), which is higher than the numbers reported for other arthropods (104 genes in D. melanogaster, 93 genes in the honey bee Apis melllifera, and 113 in the centipede Strigamia maritima) (Chipman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on identification of homeobox genes in the genome.

claim: Parhyale has an expansion to 12 CERS genes, compared to 1–4 genes found in other arthropods.
source: We observed an expansion to 12 CERS genes in Parhyale, compared to 1–4 genes found in other arthropods (Zhong and Holland, 2011) (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of CERS homeobox genes.

claim: Parhyale contains a complement of 9 canonical Hox genes that exhibit both spatial and temporal colinearity in their expression along the anterior-posterior body axis.
source: Parhyale contains a complement of 9 canonical Hox genes that exhibit both spatial and temporal colinearity in their expression along the anterior-posterior body axis (Serano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on previous characterization of Hox genes and their expression patterns.

claim: The Parhyale Hox genes labial (lab) and proboscipedia (pb) are linked.
source: Chromosome walking experiments had shown that the Hox genes labial (lab) and proboscipedia (pb) are linked and that Deformed (Dfd), Sex combs reduced (Scr), Antennapedia (Antp) and Ultrabithorax (Ubx) are also contiguous in a cluster (Serano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on previous BAC sequencing experiments.

claim: The Parhyale Hox genes Deformed (Dfd), Sex combs reduced (Scr), Antennapedia (Antp) and Ultrabithorax (Ubx) are contiguous in a cluster.
source: Chromosome walking experiments had shown that the Hox genes labial (lab) and proboscipedia (pb) are linked and that Deformed (Dfd), Sex combs reduced (Scr), Antennapedia (Antp) and Ultrabithorax (Ubx) are also contiguous in a cluster (Serano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on previous BAC sequencing experiments.

claim: FISH experiments demonstrated the linkage of lab with Dfd, Ubx and abd-A, and abd-A with Abd-B in Parhyale.
source: We then demonstrated the tightly coupled transcripts of lab with Dfd (co-expressed in the second antennal segment, Figure 10D - D"), Ubx and abd-A (co-expressed in the posterior thoracic segments, Figure 10E - E"), and abd-A with Abd-B (co-expressed in the anterior abdominal segments, (Figure 10F - F").
evidence: This is based on fluorescent in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 10.

claim: All evidence supports the linkage of all analysed Hox genes into a single cluster in Parhyale.
source: Collectively, all evidence supports the linkage of all analysed Hox genes into a single cluster as shown in (Figure 10G - G").
evidence: This is based on combining BAC sequencing and FISH data.

claim: Parhyale has 2 caudal (Cdx) and 1 Gsx ParaHox genes.
source: In Parhyale, we found 2 caudal (Cdx) and 1 Gsx ParaHox genes.
evidence: This is based on identification of ParaHox genes in the genome.

claim: Parhyale has expansions in some NK-like genes, including 5 Bar homeobox genes (BarH1/2), 2 developing brain homeobox genes (DBX) and 6 muscle segment homeobox genes (MSX/Drop).
source: Compared to hexapods, we identified expansions in some NK-like genes, including 5 Bar homeobox genes (BarH1/2), 2 developing brain homeobox genes (DBX) and 6 muscle segment homeobox genes (MSX/Drop).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of NK gene families.

claim: An NK2-3 gene and an NK3 gene are on the same scaffold in Parhyale.
source: In the current assembly of the Parhyale genome, we identified an NK2-3 gene and an NK3 gene on the same scaffold (phaw_30.0004720)
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene positions in the genome assembly.

claim: There is a tandem duplication of an NK2 gene on scaffold phaw_30.0004663 in Parhyale.
source: and the tandem duplication of an NK2 gene on another scaffold (phaw_30.0004663).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene positions in the genome assembly.

claim: Parhyale has 1 mesenchyme homeobox (Meox), 1 motor neuron homeobox (MNX/Exex) and 3 even-skipped homeobox (Evx) genes.
source: Within the ANTP class, we also observed 1 mesenchyme homeobox (Meox), 1 motor neuron homeobox (MNX/Exex) and 3 even-skipped homeobox (Evx) genes.
evidence: This is based on identification of ANTP class homeobox genes.

claim: Parhyale has 73 GH genes with complete GH catalytic domains that were classified into 17 families.
source: We identified 73 GH genes with complete GH catalytic domains that were classified into 17 families (Figure 12—source data 1) including 3 members of the GH7 family.
evidence: This is based on identification of glycosyl hydrolase genes using CAZy database classification.

claim: Parhyale has 3 members of the GH7 family.
source: We identified 73 GH genes with complete GH catalytic domains that were classified into 17 families (Figure 12—source data 1) including 3 members of the GH7 family.
evidence: This is based on identification and classification of GH7 genes.

claim: Parhyale GH7s show high sequence similarity to the known GH7 genes in L. quadripunctata and the amphipod C. terebrans.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of Parhyale GH7s show high sequence similarity to the known GH7 genes in L. quadripunctata and the amphipod C. terebrans (Kern et al., 2013) (Figure 12A; Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of GH7 protein sequences.

claim: GH7 family genes were identified in the transcriptomes of Echinogammarus veneris (amphipod), Eucyclops serrulatus (copepod) and Calanus finmarchicus (copepod).
source: GH7 family genes were also identified in the transcriptomes of three more species spanning the multicrustacea clade: Echinogammarus veneris (amphipod), Eucyclops serrulatus (copepod) and Calanus finmarchicus (copepod).
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcriptome data from other crustacean species.

claim: A closely related GH7 gene was discovered in the branchiopod Daphnia.
source: As previously reported, we also discovered a closely related GH7 gene in the branchiopod Daphnia (Figure 12A) (Cragg et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and previous reports.

claim: Parhyale has 3 GH9 family genes with complete catalytic domains.
source: We found 3 GH9 family genes with complete catalytic domains in the Parhyale genome as well as in the other three multicrustacean species (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is based on identification of GH9 genes in the genome.

claim: Parhyale has 7 beta-glucosidases from the GH30 family and 3 from the GH9 family, but none from the GH1 family.
source: In Parhyale, we found 7 beta-glucosidases from the GH30 family and 3 from the GH9 family, but none from the GH1 family.
evidence: This is based on identification and classification of beta-glucosidase genes.

claim: No PGRP genes were found in the Parhyale genome.
source: Surprisingly, we found no PGRP genes in the Parhyale genome.
evidence: This is based on searching for PGRP genes in the genome annotation.

claim: PGRPs were not found in other sequence datasets from Branchiopoda, Copepoda and Malacostraca.
source: PGRPs were also not found in other sequence datasets from Branchiopoda, Copepoda and Malacostraca (Figure 13A)
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcriptome and genome data from other crustacean species.

claim: A putative PGRP was found in the Remipede Speleonectes tulumensis.
source: Interestingly, we found a putative PGRP in the Remipede Speleonectes tulumensis (Figure 13A) providing further support for sister group relationship of Remipedia and Hexapoda (von Reumont et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of PGRP genes.

claim: Parhyale has one LGBP gene and two serine proteinases with high sequence identity to SPH1/2 in Pacifastacus.
source: In Parhyale, we found one LGBP gene and two serine proteinases with high sequence identity to SPH1/2 in Pacifastacus.
evidence: This is based on identification of immune-related genes in the genome.

claim: Parhyale has 16 members of the Toll family including 10 Toll-like receptors (TLRs).
source: We found 16 members of the Toll family in Parhyale including 10 Toll-like receptors (TLRs) (Figure 13B).
evidence: This is based on identification of Toll family genes in the genome.

claim: Parhyale has 7 Imd and 25 JAK/STAT pathway members including two negative regulators: SOCS and PIAS.
source: Additionally, we identified 7 Imd and 25 JAK/STAT pathway members including two negative regulators: suppressor of cytokine signaling (SOCS), and protein inhibitor of activated STAT (PIAS) (Arbouzova and Zeidler, 2006) (Figure 13—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on identification of immune signaling pathway genes.

claim: Parhyale has 5 TEPs (thioester-containing proteins).
source: We find 5 TEPs in the Parhyale genome.
evidence: This is based on identification of TEP genes in the genome.

claim: Parhyale has 7 phenoloxidase (PO) genes.
source: POs are involved in several biological processes (like the melanization immune response, wound healing and cuticle sclerotization) and we identified 7 PO genes in Parhyale.
evidence: This is based on identification of PO genes in the genome.

claim: The Parhyale Dscam locus has tandem arrays of multiple exons encoding the N-terminal halves of Ig2 (exon 4 array with at least 13 variants) and Ig3 (exon 6 array with at least 20 variants) and the entire Ig7 domain (exon 14 array with at least 13 variants) resulting in at least 3380 possible combinations.
source: The Dscam locus in Parhyale (and in other crustaceans analysed) has a similar organization to insects; tandem arrays of multiple exons encode the N-terminal halves of Ig2 (exon 4 array with at least 13 variants) and Ig3 (exon 6 array with at least 20 variants) and the entire Ig7 domain (exon 14 array with at least 13 variants) resulting in at least 3380 possible combinations (Figure 13C–E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Dscam gene structure in the genome.

claim: The alternative splicing of hypervariable exons in Parhyale Dscam was confirmed by sequencing of cDNA clones.
source: The alternative splicing of hypervariable exons in Parhyale was confirmed by sequencing of cDNA clones amplified with Dscam-specific primers.
evidence: This is based on experimental validation of alternative splicing.

claim: Almost the entire Parhyale Dscam gene is represented in a single genomic scaffold.
source: Almost the entire Dscam gene is represented in a single genomic scaffold and exhibits high amino-acid sequence conservation with other crustacean Dscams (Figure 13——figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the genome assembly and sequence alignments.

claim: The Parhyale genome encodes 4 argonaute family members, 2 PIWI family members, and orthologs of D. melanogaster Dicer-1 and Dicer-2, drosha and loquacious.
source: We found key components of all major small RNA pathways, including 4 argonaute family members, 2 PIWI family members, and orthologs of D. melanogaster Dicer-1 and Dicer-2, drosha and loquacious, (Figure 14—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on identification of small RNA pathway genes in the genome.

claim: Parhyale has 1 AGO-1 ortholog and 3 AGO-2 orthologs.
source: Among Argonaute genes, Parhyale has 1 AGO-1 ortholog and 3 AGO-2 orthologs, which is presumably a malacostraca-specific expansion.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of Argonaute genes.

claim: No evidence for the SID-1 transmembrane protein was found in the Parhyale genome.
source: Unlike in C. elegans, many mammals, fish and insects (but not D. melanogaster), we did not find any evidence in the Parhyale genome for the SID-1 (systemic RNA interference defective) transmembrane protein that is essential for systemic RNAi (Dong and Friedrich, 2005;Honeybee Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2006; Xu and Han, 2008).
evidence: This is based on searching for SID-1 in the genome annotation.

claim: 1405 homologues of known non-coding RNAs were annotated in Parhyale using Rfam.
source: We annotated 1405 homologues of known non-coding RNAs using Rfam.
evidence: This is based on Rfam annotation of the genome.

claim: Parhyale has 980 predicted tRNAs.
source: This includes 980 predicted tRNAs
evidence: This is based on Rfam annotation of the genome.

claim: Parhyale has 42 highly conserved miRNA genes identified by Rfam.
source: and 42 highly conserved miRNA genes (﻿﻿Source code 6).
evidence: This is based on Rfam annotation of the genome.

claim: 220,284 putative lncRNAs were identified from the Parhyale transcriptome, of which 32,223 are multi-exonic.
source: Parhyale long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) were identified from the transcriptome using a series of filters to remove coding transcripts producing a list of 220,284 putative lncRNAs (32,223 of which are multi-exonic).
evidence: This is based on filtering transcriptome data to identify non-coding RNAs.

claim: Only one Parhyale lncRNA has clear homology to another annotated lncRNA, the sphinx lncRNA from D. melanogaster.
source: Only one Parhyale lncRNA has clear homology to another annotated lncRNA, the sphinx lncRNA from D. melanogaster (Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on homology searches of lncRNAs.

claim: 1403 potential miRNA precursors represented by 100 or more reads were identified using MiRPara.
source: We identified 1403 potential miRNA precursors represented by 100 or more reads.
evidence: This is based on MiRPara analysis of small RNA sequencing data.

claim: 31 out of the 34 miRNA families found in all Bilateria were annotated in Parhyale.
source: Combining MiRPara and Rfam results, we annotated 31 out of the 34 miRNA families found in all Bilateria
evidence: This is based on combining MiRPara and Rfam results.

claim: 12 miRNAs specific to Protostomia were annotated in Parhyale.
source: 12 miRNAs specific to Protostomia
evidence: This is based on combining MiRPara and Rfam results.

claim: 4 miRNAs specific to Arthropoda were annotated in Parhyale.
source: 4 miRNAs specific to Arthropoda
evidence: This is based on combining MiRPara and Rfam results.

claim: 5 miRNAs previously found to be specific to Mandibulata were annotated in Parhyale.
source: and 5 miRNAs previously found to be specific to Mandibulata (Figure 14).
evidence: This is based on combining MiRPara and Rfam results.

claim: mir-125, mir-283 and mir-1993 were not identified in the Parhyale genome.
source: We did not identify mir-125, mir-283 and mir-1993 in the Parhyale genome.
evidence: This is based on miRNA annotation results.

claim: Parhyale mir-100 and let-7 occurred in a cluster on the same scaffold.
source: While we did not identify mir-125, we observed that mir-100 and let-7 occurred in a cluster on the same scaffold (Figure 14—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is based on analysis of miRNA positions in the genome.

claim: Parhyale mir-100 and let-7 are localized within a 9.3kb region.
source: Both genes in Parhyale are localized within a 9.3kb region (Figure 14—figure supplement 2) as compared to 3.8kb in the mosquito Anopheles gambiae and 100bp in the beetle Tribolium (Behura, 2007).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genomic distances between miRNA genes.

claim: Parhyale mir-100 and let-7 are co-transcribed as a single, polycistronic lncRNA.
source: Similar to D. melanogaster and the polychaete Platynereis dumerilii, we found that Parhyale mir-100 and let-7 are co-transcribed as a single, polycistronic lncRNA.
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcriptome data.

claim: A cluster with miR-71 and mir-2 family members was found in Parhyale, which is conserved across many invertebrates.
source: We also found another cluster with miR-71 and mir-2 family members which is conserved across many invertebrates (Marco et al., 2014) (Figure 14—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of miRNA gene positions and comparison to other species.

claim: Parhyale mir-10 is located between Dfd and Scr Hox genes.
source: In the Parhyale genome and Hox BAC sequences, we found that mir-10 is also located between Dfd and Src on BAC clone PA179-K23 and scaffold phaw_30.0001203 (Figure 14——figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene positions in the genome and BAC sequences.

claim: mir-iab-4 could not be detected near the Ubx and AbdA genes in Parhyale.
source: However, we could not detect mir-iab-4 near the Ubx and AbdA genes in Parhyale, the location where it is found in other arthropods/insects (Cumberledge et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on searching for mir-iab-4 in the Hox cluster region.

claim: The Parhyale genome encodes members of all 3 families DNMT1, DNMT3 and DNMT2.
source: The Parhyale genome encodes members of all 3 families DNMT1, DNMT3 and DNMT2, as well as 2 orthologs of conserved methyl-CpG-binding proteins and a single orthologue of Tet2, an enzyme involved in DNA demethylation (Hackett et al., 2013) (Figure 15A and Figure 15—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on identification of DNA methyltransferase genes in the genome.

claim: 20–30% of Parhyale DNA is methylated at CpG dinucleotides.
source: Our results indicated that 20–30% of Parhyale DNA is methylated at CpG dinucleotides (Figure 15B).
evidence: This is based on genome-wide bisulfite sequencing data.

claim: The Parhyale methylation pattern is similar to that observed in vertebrates, with high levels of methylation detected in transposable elements and other repetitive elements, in promoters and gene bodies.
source: The Parhyale methylation pattern is similar to that observed in vertebrates, with high levels of methylation detected in transposable elements and other repetitive elements, in promoters and gene bodies (Figure 15C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of methylation patterns across different genomic features.

claim: About 1% or less of CpG-associated cytosines are methylated in insects like Drosophila, Apis, Bombyx and Tribolium.
source: For comparison, about 1% or less of CpG-associated cytosines are methylated in insects like Drosophila, Apis, Bombyx and Tribolium. (Feng et al., 2010; Jeltsch, 2010; Zemach et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two sgRNAs targeting PhDll-e were injected individually into 1-cell-stage embryos together with Cas9, and both gave rise to animals with truncated limbs.
source: For PhDll-e knock-out, two sgRNAs targeting both alleles in their coding sequences downstream of the start codon and upstream of the DNA-binding homeodomain were injected individually into 1-cell-stage embryos (G0 generation) together with a transient source of Cas9 (Figure 16—figure supplement 1 A-B). Both sgRNAs gave rise to animals with truncated limbs (Figure 16A and B)
evidence: This is based on CRISPR/Cas9 knockout experiments.

claim: The first sgRNA targeting PhDll-e gave rise to animals with truncated limbs at a relatively low percentage around 9%.
source: the first sgRNA at a relatively low percentage around 9%
evidence: This is based on quantification of phenotypes in CRISPR experiments.

claim: The second sgRNA targeting PhDll-e gave rise to animals with truncated limbs at very high frequencies ranging between 53% and 76%.
source: and the second one at very high frequencies ranging between 53% and 76% (Figure 16—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on quantification of phenotypes in CRISPR experiments.

claim: Genotyping experiments revealed that injected embryos carried PhDll-e alleles modified at the site targeted by each sgRNA.
source: Genotyping experiments revealed that injected embryos carried PhDll-e alleles modified at the site targeted by each sgRNA (Figure 16—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on sequencing of PCR products from injected embryos.

claim: 88% (15/17) of G0 founders gave rise to G1 offspring with truncated limbs.
source: In one experiment with the most efficient sgRNA, we raised the injected animals to adulthood and set pairwise crosses between 17 fertile G0s (10 male and 7 female): 88% (15/17) of these founders gave rise to G1 offspring with truncated limbs, presumably by transmitting PhDll-e alleles modified by Cas9 in their germlines.
evidence: This is based on breeding experiments with CRISPR-injected animals.

claim: G1 embryos bearing truncated limbs were homozygous for loss-of-function alleles with out-of-frame deletions.
source: We tested this by genotyping individual G1s from two of these crosses and found that embryos bearing truncated limbs were homozygous for loss-of-function alleles with out-of-frame deletions
evidence: This is based on genotyping of G1 offspring.

claim: Wild-type G1 siblings carried one loss-of-function allele and one functional allele with an in-frame deletion.
source: while their wild-type siblings carried one loss-of-function allele and one functional allele with an in-frame deletion (Figure 16—figure supplement 1 D).
evidence: This is based on genotyping of G1 offspring.

claim: About 7% of injected G0s exhibited a nuclear fluorescence signal in the distal parts of developing appendages in the knock-in experiment.
source: Among injected G0s, about 7% exhibited a nuclear fluorescence signal in the distal (telopodite and exopodite) parts of developing appendages (Figure 16C and Figure 16—figure supplement 1 E)
evidence: This is based on screening for fluorescence in CRISPR knock-in experiments.

claim: Genotyping of a fluorescent embryo demonstrated that the tagged PhDll-e locus was encoding a functional PhDll-e protein with a small in-frame deletion around the targeted region.
source: Genotyping of one of these embryos demonstrated that the tagged PhDll-e locus was indeed encoding a functional PhDll-e protein with a small in-frame deletion around the targeted region (Figure 16—figure supplement 1 F).
evidence: This is based on sequencing of junction PCR products from fluorescent embryos.

claim: Recent molecular and morphological studies have placed crustaceans along with hexapods into a pancrustacean clade, revealing that crustaceans are paraphyletic.
source: Recent molecular and morphological studies have placed crustaceans along with hexapods into a pancrustacean clade (Figure 1A), revealing that crustaceans are paraphyletic (Mallatt et al., 2004; Cook et al., 2005; Regier et al., 2005; Ertas et al., 2009; Richter, 2002).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Previously, the only available fully sequenced crustacean genome was that of the water flea Daphnia which is a member of the Branchiopoda.
source: Previously, the only available fully sequenced crustacean genome was that of the water flea Daphnia which is a member of the Branchiopoda (Colbourne et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of crustacean genomics prior to this work.

claim: The genome of the amphipod crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis addresses the paucity of high quality non-hexapod genomes among the pancrustacean group.
source: The genome of the amphipod crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis addresses the paucity of high quality non-hexapod genomes among the pancrustacean group, and will help to resolve relationships within this group as more genomes and complete proteomes become available (Rivarola-Duarte et al., 2014; Kenny et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the Parhyale genome.

claim: Genome sequence data is necessary to further advance research in Parhyale, particularly for the application of powerful functional genomic approaches, such as genome editing.
source: Crucially, genome sequence data is also necessary to further advance research in Parhyale, currently the most tractable crustacean model system. This is particularly true for the application of powerful functional genomic approaches, such as genome editing (Cong et al., 2013; Serano et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2015; Mali et al., 2013; Jinek et al., 2012; Gilles and Averof, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the genome for functional studies.

claim: Parhyale is a direct developer.
source: Parhyale is a direct developer and a sexually dimorphic species.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend describing the life cycle.

claim: Parhyale is a sexually dimorphic species.
source: Parhyale is a direct developer and a sexually dimorphic species.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend describing the life cycle.

claim: The fertilized Parhyale egg undergoes stereotyped total cleavages and each blastomere becomes committed to a particular germ layer already at the 8-cell stage.
source: The fertilized egg undergoes stereotyped total cleavages and each blastomere becomes committed to a particular germ layer already at the 8-cell stage depicted in (D).
evidence: This is a description of early Parhyale development.

claim: The three macromeres Er, El, and Ep give rise to the anterior right, anterior left, and posterior ectoderm, respectively, in Parhyale.
source: The three macromeres Er, El, and Ep give rise to the anterior right, anterior left, and posterior ectoderm, respectively
evidence: This describes the fate of specific blastomeres in Parhyale.

claim: The fourth macromere Mav gives rise to the visceral mesoderm and anterior head somatic mesoderm in Parhyale.
source: while the fourth macromere Mav gives rise to the visceral mesoderm and anterior head somatic mesoderm.
evidence: This describes the fate of a specific blastomere in Parhyale.

claim: Among the 4 micromeres in Parhyale, the mr and ml micromeres give rise to the right and left somatic trunk mesoderm.
source: Among the 4 micromeres, the mr and ml micromeres give rise to the right and left somatic trunk mesoderm
evidence: This describes the fate of specific blastomeres in Parhyale.

claim: The en micromere gives rise to the endoderm in Parhyale.
source: en gives rise to the endoderm
evidence: This describes the fate of a specific blastomere in Parhyale.

claim: The g micromere gives rise to the germline in Parhyale.
source: and g gives rise to the germline.
evidence: This describes the fate of a specific blastomere in Parhyale.

claim: Members of the Malacostraca, specifically both Amphipods and Isopods, are thought to be capable of lignocellulose digestion and to have microbiota-free digestive systems.
source: In addition, members of the Malacostraca, specifically both Amphipods and Isopods, are thought to be capable of 'wood eating' or lignocellulose digestion and to have microbiota-free digestive systems (King et al., 2010; Kern et al., 2013; Boyle and Mitchell, 1978; Zimmer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Gravid Parhyale females lay eggs every 2 weeks upon reaching sexual maturity.
source: Gravid females lay eggs every 2 weeks upon reaching sexual maturity and hundreds of eggs can be easily collected at all stages of embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a description of Parhyale reproductive biology.

claim: Parhyale embryogenesis takes about 10 days at 26°C.
source: Embryogenesis takes about 10 days at 26°C and has been described in detail with an accurate staging system (Browne et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a description of Parhyale developmental timing.

claim: Early Parhyale embryos display an invariant cell lineage with each blastomere at the 8-cell stage contributing to a specific germ layer.
source: Early embryos display an invariant cell lineage with each blastomere at the 8-cell stage contributing to a specific germ layer (Figure 1D) (Browne et al., 2005; Gerberding et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on previous lineage tracing studies.

claim: The utility of the CRISPR/Cas system for targeted genome editing has been elegantly demonstrated during the systematic study of Parhyale Hox genes.
source: Most recently the utility of the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas) system for targeted genome editing has been elegantly demonstrated during the systematic study of Parhyale Hox genes (Martin et al., 2015; Serano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on recent publications on CRISPR in Parhyale.

claim: The high number of predicted gene models and proteins in Parhyale is almost certainly an overestimation due to fragmented genes, very different isoforms or unresolved alleles.
source: Almost certainly the high number of predicted gene models and proteins is an overestimation due to fragmented genes, very different isoforms or unresolved alleles, that will be consolidated as annotation of the Parhyale genome improves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the challenges of assembling a highly heterozygous genome.

claim: The big size of the Parhyale genome can be in large part attributed to the expansion of repetitive sequences.
source: We also observed a frequency of repeat branches approximately 4x higher than those observed in both the human and oyster genomes (Figure 3C), suggesting that the big size of the Parhyale genome can be in large part attributed to the expansion of repetitive sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on k-mer analysis of repeat content.

claim: The expansion of repetitive sequences and the increase in gene size due to an expansion of intron size have contributed to the large size of the Parhyale genome.
source: Our comparative bioinformatics analyses suggest that the expansion of repetitive sequences and the increase in gene size due to an expansion of intron size have contributed to the large size of the genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Within captive laboratory populations of Parhyale there is considerable additional polymorphism distributed across genes.
source: This analysis suggests that within captive laboratory populations of Parhyale there is considerable additional polymorphism distributed across genes, irrespective of whether or not they have relatively low or high heterozygosity in the individual male we sequenced.
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcriptome data from multiple populations.

claim: The single male Parhyale sequenced provides an accurate reflection of polymorphism of the wider laboratory population.
source: In addition the single male we have sequenced provides an accurate reflection of polymorphism of the wider laboratory population and the established Chicago-F strain does not by chance contain unusually divergent haplotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of genome and transcriptome polymorphism.

claim: Special attention will have to be given to functional genomic approaches that are dependent on homology, such as CRISPR/Cas9 based knock in strategies, due to high levels of polymorphism in Parhyale.
source: Taken togther these data mean that special attention will have to be given to those functional genomic approaches that are dependent on homology, such as CRISPR/Cas9 based knock in strategies.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of high polymorphism for genome editing.

claim: The presence of GH7 genes and the absence of PGRP genes in branchiopod and multicrustacean genomes support the Vericrustacea hypothesis.
source: While the analysis of shared orthologous groups did not provide clear support for either the Allotriocarida hypothesis (uniting Branchiopoda with Hexapoda) or the Vericrustacea hypothesis (uniting Branchiopoda with Malacostraca), we noted the presence of GH7 genes and the absence of PGRP genes in branchiopod and multicrustacean genomes supporting the Vericrustacea hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of specific gene families.

claim: The finding of GH7 genes in Parhyale and other multicrustacea supports the grouping of Branchiopoda with Multicrustacea.
source: This finding supports the grouping of Branchiopoda with Multicrustacea (rather than with Hexapoda) and the acquisition of a GH7 gene by a vericrustacean ancestor.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution of GH7 genes.

claim: The acquisition of a GH7 gene may have occurred by a crustacean ancestor with subsequent loss of the GH7 family gene in the lineage leading to insects.
source: Alternatively, this suggests an even earlier acquisition of a GH7 gene by a crustacean ancestor with subsequent loss of the GH7 family gene in the lineage leading to insects.
evidence: This is an alternative evolutionary scenario inferred from gene distribution.

claim: The absence of PGRP genes raises the possibility of a close phylogenetic relationship between Branchiopoda and Multicrustacea.
source: Surprisingly, we found no PGRP genes in the Parhyale genome. PGRPs were also not found in other sequence datasets from Branchiopoda, Copepoda and Malacostraca (Figure 13A), raising the possibility of their close phylogenetic relationship (like the GH7 genes).
evidence: This is an inference based on the shared absence of PGRP genes.

claim: The finding of a putative PGRP in the Remipede Speleonectes tulumensis provides further support for sister group relationship of Remipedia and Hexapoda.
source: Interestingly, we found a putative PGRP in the Remipede Speleonectes tulumensis (Figure 13A) providing further support for sister group relationship of Remipedia and Hexapoda (von Reumont et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of PGRP in Remipedia.

claim: The number of Dscam isoforms predicted in Parhyale is similar to that predicted for Daphnia species.
source: The number of Dscam isoforms predicted in Parhyale is similar to that predicted for Daphnia species (Brites et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on analysis of Dscam gene structure.

claim: It remains an open question whether the higher number of isoforms observed in insects coincides with the evolution of additional Dscam functions compared to crustaceans.
source: It remains an open question whether the higher number of isoforms observed in insects coincides with the evolution of additional Dscam functions compared to crustaceans.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of Dscam diversity.

claim: Species without a SID-1 ortholog can silence genes only in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Species without a SID-1 ortholog can silence genes only in a cell-autonomous manner (Roignant et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on previous studies of RNAi mechanisms.

claim: The absence of SID-1 has important implications for future design of RNAi experiments in Parhyale.
source: This feature has important implications for future design of RNAi experiments in Parhyale.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical implications of the absence of SID-1.

claim: The absence of mir-1993 in Parhyale is consistent with reports that this miRNA was lost during Arthropod evolution.
source: The absence of mir-1993 is consistent with reports that this miRNA was lost during Arthropod evolution (Wheeler et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on comparison to previous phylogenetic studies of miRNAs.

claim: The absence of mir-125 has been also reported for the centipede genome.
source: The absence of mir-125 has been also reported for the centipede genome (Chipman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on previous genome studies.

claim: mir-100 is one of the most primitive miRNAs shared by Bilateria and Cnidaria.
source: mir-100 is one of the most primitive miRNAs shared by Bilateria and Cnidaria (Grimson et al., 2008; Wheeler et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic studies of miRNA evolution.

claim: The distance between mir-100 and let-7 genes within the cluster can vary substantially between different species.
source: The distance between mir-100 and let-7 genes within the cluster can vary substantially between different species.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of miRNA gene positions.

claim: The phylogenetically conserved mir-10 is present within both vertebrate and invertebrate Hox clusters between Hoxb4/Dfd and Hoxb5/Scr.
source: For example, the phylogenetically conserved mir-10 is present within both vertebrate and invertebrate Hox clusters between Hoxb4/Dfd and Hoxb5/Scr (Enright et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is based on previous studies of miRNA-Hox gene linkage.

claim: The bilaterian ancestor had at least one member of the Dnmt1 and Dnmt3 families and the Dnmt2 family, as well as additional RNA methyltransferases.
source: The phylogenetic distribution of DNMTs in Metazoa suggests that the bilaterian ancestor had at least one member of the Dnmt1 and Dnmt3 families (involved in de novo methylation and maintenance of DNA methylation) and the Dnmt2 family (involved in tRNA methylation), as well as additional RNA methyltransferases (Jones and Liang, 2009; Jeltsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of DNMT genes.

claim: Many animal groups have lost some DNA methyltransferases, for example DNMT1 and 3 are absent from D. melanogaster and flatworms.
source: Many animal groups have lost some of these DNA methyltransferases, for example DNMT1 and 3 are absent from D. melanogaster and flatworms (Goll et al., 2006; Jaber-Hijazi et al., 2013)
evidence: This is based on previous studies of DNMT gene distribution.

claim: DNMT2 is absent from nematodes C. elegans and C. briggsae.
source: while DNMT2 is absent from nematodes C. elegans and C. briggsae.
evidence: This is based on previous studies of DNMT gene distribution.

claim: A particular class of rolling-circle transposons are very highly methylated in the Parhyale genome, potentially implicating methylation in silencing these elements.
source: A particular class of rolling-circle transposons are very highly methylated in the genome, potentially implicating methylation in silencing these elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of high methylation in rolling-circle transposons.

claim: These data represent the first documentation of a crustacean methylome.
source: These data represent the first documentation of a crustacean methylome.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the methylation data.

claim: The ability to manipulate the fertilized eggs together with the slow tempo of early cleavages can result in very high targeting frequencies and low levels of mosaicism for both knock-out and knock-in approaches in Parhyale.
source: These results, together with the other recent applications of the CRISPR/Cas system to study Hox genes in Parhyale (Martin et al., 2015; Serano et al., 2015), demonstrate that the ability to manipulate the fertilized eggs together with the slow tempo of early cleavages can result in very high targeting frequencies and low levels of mosaicism for both knock-out and knock-in approaches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CRISPR experiments presented and previous work.

claim: The Parhyale embryo will prove an extremely powerful system for fast and reliable G0 screens of gene expression and function.
source: Considering the usefulness of the genome-wide resources described in this report, we anticipate that the Parhyale embryo will prove an extremely powerful system for fast and reliable G0 screens of gene expression and function.
evidence: This is a speculation about the future utility of Parhyale for functional genomics.

claim: Parhyale provides an excellent arthropod model system to understand the enigmatic phenomena of Hox gene clustering and spatio-temporal colinearity.
source: Despite these caveats, Parhyale provides an excellent arthropod model system to understand these still enigmatic phenomena of Hox gene clustering and spatio-temporal colinearity, and compare the underlying mechanisms to other well-studied vertebrate and invertebrate models (Kmita and Duboule, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of Parhyale for studying Hox gene regulation.

claim: In some respects, including the segmented body plan, the presence of a blood system and the contribution of lineage-committed adult stem cells to newly formed tissues, regeneration in Parhyale may resemble the process in vertebrates more than other established invertebrate models.
source: In some respects, including the segmented body plan, the presence of a blood system and the contribution of lineage-committed adult stem cells to newly formed tissues, regeneration in Parhyale may resemble the process in vertebrates more than other established invertebrate models (e.g. planarians, hydra).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about regeneration mechanisms.

claim: Regenerative research in Parhyale has been founded on transgenic approaches to label specific populations of cells.
source: Regenerative research in Parhyale has been founded on transgenic approaches to label specific populations of cells and will be further assisted by the resources presented here.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in Parhyale regeneration research.

claim: The new genomic information and CRISPR-based genome editing methodologies together with all other facets of Parhyale biology will open other new research avenues not yet imagined.
source: Likewise, we expect that the new genomic information and CRISPR-based genome editing methodologies together with all other facets of Parhyale biology will open other new research avenues not yet imagined.
evidence: This is a speculation about the future impact of the Parhyale genome.

claim: A deeper mechanistic understanding of the Parhyale immune system will be relevant to aquaculture.
source: Besides the evolutionary implications and the characterization of alternative strategies used by arthropods to defend against pathogens, a deeper mechanistic understanding of the Parhyale immune system will be relevant to aquaculture.
evidence: This is an inference about the applied relevance of Parhyale immunity research.

claim: Some of the greatest setbacks in the crustacean farming industry are caused by severe disease outbreaks.
source: Some of the greatest setbacks in the crustacean farming industry are caused by severe disease outbreaks.
evidence: This is a statement about problems in aquaculture.

claim: Parhyale is closely related to farmed crustaceans (primarily shrimps, prawns and crayfish).
source: Parhyale is closely related to farmed crustaceans (primarily shrimps, prawns and crayfish)
evidence: This is a statement about the phylogenetic relationship of Parhyale to aquaculture species.

claim: Knowledge acquired from studying Parhyale innate immunity could help enhance the sustainability of the crustacean farming industry by preventing or controlling infectious diseases.
source: and the knowledge acquired from studying its innate immunity could help enhance the sustainability of this industry by preventing or controlling infectious diseases (Stentiford et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2008; Rajesh Kumar et al., 2008; Rowley and Pope, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference about the applied relevance of Parhyale immunity research.

claim: Parhyale, like limnoriid Isopods, encodes and expresses all enzymes required for lignocellulose digestion.
source: Parhyale, like limnoriid Isopods, encodes and expresses all enzymes required for lignocellulose digestion, suggesting that it is able to 'digest wood' by itself without symbiotic microbial partners.
evidence: This is based on the identification of glycosyl hydrolase genes in the genome.

claim: The possibility of an experimentally tractable animal model that serves as a living bioreactor to convert lignocellulose into simpler metabolites suggests that future research in Parhyale may have a strong biotechnological potential, especially for the production of biofuels from plant biomass.
source: Nevertheless, the possibility of an experimentally tractable animal model that serves as a living bioreactor to convert lignocellulose into simpler metabolites, suggests that future research in Parhyale may also have a strong biotechnological potential, especially for the production of biofuels from the most abundant and cheapest raw material, plant biomass.
evidence: This is a speculation about the biotechnological potential of Parhyale.
